subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset may I associate myself with previous speakers in congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) on his admirable presentation of one of the best budgets to which I have been privileged to listen in the House of Commons. It was comprehensive and so lucid that the man on the street could understand it. Anyone reading or hearing it would realize that drastic remedies were necessary were Canada to meet her obligations and to hold her present high position among the nations of the earth, and he suggested the necessary remedies.
Before proceeding further with the budget debate I wish, without too great a trespass on the patience of the house, to take up a matter with relation to British Columbia. As is known, strong comments were made with respect to the provincial government regarding the disbursement of unemployment relief funds in that province. Before I came to the defence of my friends "of many days and in many ways," I waited the findings of a commission that was sitting in British Columbia. Doctor Tolmie, as hon. members know, is premier of that province. We thrust him into
The Budget-Mr. Dickie

that position against his wishes. The electorate there were sick and tired to death of Liberal rule and we cast around to find some man popular enough to unite our two factions. Doctor Tolmie, because of his splendid personality and reputation we knew could do the trick, we gave him the third degree and absolutely forced him to accept the premiership of British Columbia. This he did, and he has been doing his best ever since. In his position, as premier, he has a great deal to do with unemployment matters. The minister in charge of unemployment relief funds in British Columbia is the Hon. Ralf Bruhn, a man who has played hard games with the forests of that province, a practical man. No one has ever done anything to impeach his honesty, and only honourable motives have been attributed to him. Mistakes were made, as would doubtless be the case in enterprises of this kind; it was a rush order; but I could point out mistakes that have been made by private and public companies in that province that would dwarf into insignificance the mistakes made by the provincial government. A parliamentary commission was appointed to inquire into the accusations made against the local government. This commission was composed of a number of Liberals as well as Conservatives, the latter of course, being in the majority. It has concluded its investigation and I am going to ask the house kindly to bear with me while I read its findings, as follows:
Charges of extravagance and irregularities preferred by members of the House of Commons and others were also investigated. The following are typical examples:
(a) "That camps were equipped with radios." Your committee finds that no radios were purchased or rented. A carload of camp food and supplies, packed by ,the shipper in cases onoe used for radios, probably led to this belief.
_ (b) "That camps were also equipped with pianos." Your committee finds that none were purchased or rented.
(c)	"That edge-grained fir floor lumber, at a cost of $74 per thousand, was used in making tables for camps." Your committee finds that the total expended on edge-grained fir floor lumber was $2.24.
(d)	"That a Vancouver firm quoted the purchasing agent a price on 10,000 blankets and that these blankets were later purchased through someone else for the government at a figure considerably in advance of that sum." Your committee finds that a total of 7,700 pair of blankets was purchased from the West Coast Woollen Mills, Limited, Vancouver, and an emergency purchase of 450 pair of blankets was made from Turner-Beaton, Victoria. All of those blankets were seven-pound blankets, purchased for the sum of 66 cents per pound. This figure was considerably less than that quoted for blankets similar in quality, by the Vancouver firm in question.
(Mr. Dickie.1
It is worthy of note that the West Coast Woollen Mills, Limited, is a concern financed by the provincial Department of Industries and that the purchase of these blankets meant not only assistance to an undertaking in which the province was financially interested but meant also that these blankets were made entirely of B.C. wool and by B.C. workmen.
The suggestion made by Mr. Thos. Reid, member of the House of Commons for New Westminster (at page 1180 of Hansard, 1932), that one manufacturer had "sold 50,000 blankets and it took him out of the red," is without any foundation in fact.
(e)	The Dominion representative in his evidence stated: "That 104 carpenters were on the pay-rolls for the camp at Deroehe on October 16 or 17, 1931, and four only working as such."
The original time-books and pay-rolls for the months of September and October were produced to your committee, and on the dates in question 47 and 37 carpenters respectively were shown in the time-books and carried on the pay-rolls, for a total of seven camps. The maximum number shown for any single day in the month of October was 79. The evidence further indicated that all worked as carpenters throughout their period of employment as such.
(f)	Mr. A. W. Neill, member of the House of Commons for Alberni, on February the 10th, 1932 (on page 90 of Hansard, 1932), made the following statement referring to oamps:

"One might say they were equipped almost luxuriously with hot and cold water shower baths, electric lighting plants, and I am informed even radios have been provided in some eases. The tools were furnished on a scale never known before in connection with road work. Every man had enough tools to suffice for ten; every man had a wheelbarrow; every man had a ten-foot saw. which was entirely unnecessary, and everything was done on a lavish scale. The material, Mr. Speaker, was all bought at the right place, you may depend. We have instances of blankets being bought at gift stores. I take it, sir, that you know what a gift store is, but if by chance you do not know may I explain it is a place where the word gift is terminated with an "e," and -where one may buy trinkets for bridge parties, and things of that nature. Blankets were bought at such places for road camps." Your committee finds that the camps were built and equipped in accordance with the regulations of the Health Act of British Columbia, and regulations for the sanitary control of lumber, mining and other camps, sawmills and other industries, and were similar, both as to cost and equipment, to oamps used by contractors and lumber men for similar numbers, purposes and periods. The showers referred to are required by the regulations aforesaid and were installed at the rate of one to 20 or 25 men, at a cost of $7 per shower; the construction consisted of tar-papered partitions with slats on the floor and wooden drains. Twenty-three "Delco" lighting plants were installed; a number of these were purchased second-hand and have a high salvage value. The cost of lighting by electric light was carefully estimated and it was found that, in large permanent camps, electric light was the most economical of all available systems and also greatly reduced the fire hazard.
The charges regarding radios and blankets have already been dealt with.

The Budget-Mr. Dickie
The evidence indicated that there was a wheelbarrow for every tenth man and a crosscut saw for every seventeenth man.
Your committee finds that the purchase of tools was on a reasonable basis and sufficient only for the number which the province reasonably expected to employ under the unemployment relief program.
Your committee finds that materials of all classes were bought from citizens of this prov-vince without regard to political leanings; instances were brought before the committee of large purchases from prominent Liberals in this province.
It should be noted that there were individual camps which contained large quantities of supplies; these were, however, used as depots, and tools were distributed therefrom as and when required by other camps in the particular neighbourhood.
(g)	Mr. Thomas Reid (at page 1283 of Hansard 1932), stated:
"I counted in one camp 450 steel wheelbarrows. They had so many that a man was to be appointed to regulate their use." The evidence before your committee indicated that there might be 450 steel wheelbarrows in one camp but it would be in the nature of a depot or warehouse camp for a group of camps, and that the man referred to would be for the purpose of distributing wheelbarrows and other tools and supplies among the various camps requiring them.	.
Mr. Reid further stated: "I have no comment to make regarding the construction camps except to criticize the loose way in which they were run." The evidence before your committee indicated that the camps were conducted in an efficient and economical manner.
That is all I have to say on that matter, Mr. Speaker, I wished to put this on Hansard for the instruction of those people who listened to charges against the British Columbia government in the debate now long passed.
With respect to the budget speech, it was an admirable presentation. For three weeks we had been listening to another very tiring eruption of words, and we listened in vain for some suggestion that would assist the government in the very difficult task with which it is now faced in the matter of unemployment, but no sound suggestion was made. The suggestion was made by the Minister of Labour in the late government, the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Heenan) that a fund of $90,000,000 be created for unemployment insurance, the federal government contributing $30,000,000, the employers $30,000,000, and the balance of $30,000,000 being contributed by the working men of this country. I would ask any manufacturer, any man who is engaged in the lumber business, for instance, I would ask the two good, practical men I know on the other side of the house, the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Munn) and the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Hanson) , what they would think of the manufacturers and industrialists of this country being asked at the present time to raise $30,000,000 for that purpose. We all realize the hardships that exist with respect to unemployment, and there may come a time, when this government gets the ship back on an even keel, when we may be able to do something along that line, or at all events do something more for labour than we are doing at the present time, but just now it is absolutely silly to talk of creating a fund of $90,000,000 to guarantee wages to men who are unemployed. The unemployment question is undoubtedly a very serious one, and a little later, if I have time,
I shall deal with it more fully.
We also had that old man of the sea, free trade, again thrust upon us during the three weeks' debate to which I have referred. It is needless to spend any time combating free trade arguments for practically every nation in the world has gone off the free trade list. Even Great Britain has abandoned free trade. What would Canada do, with a population of ten million people, living alongside a highly protected nation of one hundred and twenty million people if we did not have a protectionist policy? We would go down and out. Had we not raised our tariff barriers during the severe times of the past year and a half, our country would have been flooded with manufactured articles from the United States and we would have had more idle working men in this country than we have at the present time. By raising our tariffs we are now buying something like one hundred million dollars' worth less of goods from the United States. That means that that one hundred million dollars is kept in this country for the benefit of Canadian working men. We hope that the government will continue to act along the same lines and protect this country. Whether theoretically protection is right or not, protection is necessary in the present state of affairs throughout the world.
Then a back-to-the-land movement was suggested. It has been advocated that owing to the tremendous number of unemployed people we have in this country we should institute a policy of getting them back on the land. We have tried that policy in a small way in British Columbia. We have been trying to do our utmost for the benefit of those men who had gone overseas and done so much for us, but this back-to-the-land movement I regret to say has not been a success in British Columbia. The back-to-the-land movement may later on prove to be a success throughout Canada if people become more inclined to go back to the simple life, but at the present time we could not place a sufficient number of men back on the land to
The Budget-Mr. Dickie

relieve the unemployment problem throughout Canada to any great extent. But we want them back there. They are better there than they would be thronging the cities, and the time may come when we can induce more of them to go back to the land. It would be a wonderful thing if we could get them out of the cities into the God-given air of the country, where their lungs would have a chance to expand and they would have different ideals than they have in the city. We have become unmoralized, if I may use the word, Mr. Speaker, by salacious literature and by rotten Hollywood films. Our people have been demoralized by bright lights and rubber tires, and the sooner we can get them away out of the cities into the pure atmosphere of the country the better. It is a big problem and I hope that we shall be able to succeed in solving it. It is a long, far cry, but the gap must be bridged between lipsticks and lips kissed with the morning dew. Get them out into the country, into the pure air and doubtless our race will be benefited thereby. In the present age we require some Virgil to teach the dignity of life in the country, someone to teach our people to get out in the God-given air, among good, pure surroundings. Nothing in this world will do as much for our population as the simple country life. We have all read of the expression of little Pippa "God's in his heaven and all's well with the world" when for the first time she went out into the country.
Mr. Speaker, I am becoming somewhat confused and I am afraid I shall have to branch off on another argument.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have very grave problems with respect to unemployment. Due to the advance of science there are many thousands of men without work. In the great nation to the south of us I understand there are 8,000,000 workless people; I do not know how they are going to be employed. There was a time when the markets of the world were open to that great country; they went full speed ahead; tremendous industrial enterprises were undertaken. At the present time each nation is protecting itself against the inroads of manufactured articles from the United States. In that country there are, as I have said, from 6,000,000 to 8,000,000 people which constitutes a grave problem. We in Canada, I am told, have about 500,000 unemployed. Although our country has a smaller population than has the United States we 
have greater undeveloped resources. The time will come no doubt when all our men will be given work. At the present time it is very difficult to see how such a condition may be brought about. I do not know, however, how the United States will ever find employment for their idle population. There may come a time when the arguments advanced by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) may have to be adopted throughout the American continent and the world. Due to the advent of labour saving machinery, the use of steam, and the use of engines capable of drawing as many care as, in the early days, three locomotives would have drawn, one man does the work of ten. It is unfortunate that the man getting along in years should be penalized through the use of labour saving machinery. The fact is, however, that there are too many labourers in the world at the present time. What must he done to remedy the situation is a matter agitating the minds of some of our greatest thinkers. I believe the day will come when two shifts of working men will do what one shift is doing to-day. I do not see any other way of putting our unemployed to work.
It is pitiful to read of the distress prevalent throughout the various cities in the United States and Canada. We are doing our best for them; measures are being enacted to give temporary relief. We want, however, to give relief which will enable them to look forward to the proper rearing of their families; we want to make those people good citizens. The leader of our party, and doubtless that of the party opposite, are agitated, trying, striving to reach a solution of our unemployment problem. Those men must have work if we are to prevent mischievous doctrines from permeating their minds. None of us would like to see in operation the doctrine proclaimed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North 'Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). We want Canada to be a country where a man may prosper according to his integrity and ability. We do not want to place people in one class as is done in Russia to-day, to do away with initiative, and to do away with all that builds good citizenship. If mankind is to improve it must have some object for which to strive.
I can remember a time when the Indians in British Columbia were almost a truly socialistic people. I remember one Indian who for some unforeseen reason, or by some piece of luck, had accumulated a little more than his fellows. As a result he gave what was known as a potlatch, and gave away everything he had. He reduced his means to a point as low or lower than those

The Royal Assent
of the rest of the band. He was called a chief, or something of that nature, and was well pleased at the return given him for his sacrifice. After he had given away his means he wrapped his blanket around him, sat in the sunshine beside his rancherie, to wait for the next run of dog salmon so that he might get enough to eat. There are some very beautiful ideals connected with socialism. We cannot however do away with initiative, or we will go down, down the line until we finally reach the primordial ooze from which we came in the first instance. We must progress, and must have some reward in view. We do not necessarily need to attack the principles of our fellow man, but must do something for our country and ourselves, if we are to survive. We want no fallacious argument of socialism to permeate this good land of ours. Ideal as a socialistic condition may seem, it does away with initiative. In Russia to-day there are millions who have nothing to look forward to. There are men without smiles going about their business, half clad and half fed. True, some few have gained notoriety as there would be if we in this country adopted a similar system. Thank God however for good Anglo Saxon common sense which permeates the minds of our people.
As hon. members are aware, an economic conference is to be held in Ottawa in July of this year. We know not what the outcome may be, but we do know that earnest men are coming from all parts of the empire to confer and reason one with the other as to what can best be done for the country and the empire as a whole.
It is too early to predict what may happen, but we know they are meeting here with the very best of intentions. There will have to be a little give and take on the part of all the various units of the British Empire, but doubtless good will result, and if we achieve one-half of what we expect we shall do away with the unemployment problem in the empire. Let us deal within the British Empire as much as possible; let us buy goods from our sister dominions and sell to them what we can manufacture to better advantage than they, and we shall soon do away with unemployment. If not, we must adopt some other measures. I know of no other government in the world that is giving more attention to this problem than the present government. The government are looking for suggestions from the other side rather than destructive criticism, they are striving to do something for the workingmen of this country. I think the most piteous feature of unemployment is the man, hollow-eyed, looking for

work and unable to get it. We do not want the minds of our people permeated with the mischievous doctrines advanced by the member for Winnipeg North Centre; we want them to be upstanding citizens, not relying on the efforts of others, but climbing up unaided to improve their position and at the same time improve this great country.
Under the wise guidance of our leader, I feel sure that he and his colleagues will solve our major problems. We stand solidly behind him, and we hope he may be spared to put Canada back in that condition of prosperity which we have every reason to expect because of the wonderful potentialities of our great natural resources. We are going to make of Canada a country worth while to live in, and I am confident we shall emerge from the present depression perhaps quicker than any other country under the sun, due to the virilitj' of our people and our great natural endowments. Then let us be careful not to drift under the influence of the indulgent gales so far from the shores of economic sanity as we did during the past, let us conserve our resources, let us go a little slower, and we shall make this one of the greatest countries in the world.
I think no other statesman of to-day has the adaptability and the qualifications so necessary for extricating Canada from the economic morass in which it is now engulfed as has our admirable leader, that right hon. gentleman:
Whose slow, wise smile,
Half within and half without
Seems filled with knowledge of the world.
He will bring us out of the impasse, and under his wise guidance we shall emerge from this depression quicker than any other country in the world. I think the economic conference next July will have an important bearing on the future of this country. If our right hon. leader extricates Canada from the tremendous burden under which we are struggling, I might say in the words of Horace, he will have:
-builded a monument Stronger than brass and of vast extent, Higher than Egypt's chief pyramid,
That monument to kingly pride;
Whose top as heaven is high,
At base as earth is wide.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad of this opportunity offered to me, of expressing my views on the budget brought down by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes). First, I wish to congratulate him on his appointment to this high office. I further desire to congratulate the hon. member for St. Anne's (Mr. Sullivan) on his maiden speech in this house.
He highly praises this budget, and adds that all the prominent financiers of this country have approved of it and stated that it was a genuine budget. I do not share the views of the hon. member for St. Anne's. He represents a constituency comprising in the major part workmen earning small wages; were he to call from door to door so as to ascertain the opinion of his electors on the budget, I think his views would soon change.
I wish, incidentally, to point out the figures quoted a few days ago by the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Gordon). He stated that the government had made an outlay of 140,000,000 to relieve unemployment and had undertaken to make a further outlay of $16,000,000 this year. I am amazed that they are disbursing such large amounts for unemployment relief; not that I am opposed to this expenditure-on the contrary, I approve of it-because I contend that the government do not practise what they advocate. The appropriations for the Department of Public Works amounted to $20,480,550, in 1931-32, and they have been cut to $13,187,000 for 1932-33, which means a reduction of more than $7,000,000. If the government were in earnest they would increase the appropriation for public works. It would be an excellent way to alleviate unemployment. After requesting the municipalities to do their utmost in helping the unemployed,
I think the government is showing a poor 
example in cutting down by $7,000,000 the estimates of the Public Works department.
The other day while glancing over a pamphlet distributed by the Minister of Labour, I discovered that in the county of Chambly-Vereheres-which is adjacent to my own and for the most part a farming county -there was expended to relieve unemployment an amount of $129,172; however, the total expenditure for the province of Quebec only amounted to $415,606. I therefore state that 'Chambly-Vereheres was more favoured than the other counties of Quebec. I do not know if it is because the constituency is represented by the Minister of Marine, who must have a great deal of influence with his colleagues, however, that county received more than 30 per cent of the amount allotted to Quebec.
The county of St. John's-Iberville, which I have the honour of representing in the House, received slightly more than $16,000. An amount of $1,210 was granted to the town of Iberville, and only $282.70 were expended, to date, for a population of more than 3,000. An expenditure of $16,195 was made in the city of St. John's which comprises more than 12,000 people and has over 900 unemployed. I contend, sir, that there has been undoubted evidence of favouritism in connection with the distribution of the unemployment funds. When I note that in the county of Chambly-Vereheres, in villages comprising between 150 and 200 people, over $6,000 were expended; in Chambly more than $19,000; in Longueuil the population of which is much less than St. John's, almost $20,000 were expended and at St. Lambert more than $69,000, I must protest on behalf of St. John's-Iberville, and state that my county like many others in Quebec, has not been given an amount of relief proportionate to the county of Chambly-Ver-cheres.
I am pleased, sir, to see the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sutherland) in his seat; as I am aware that he understands the beautiful French language, I wish to point out to him that in the budget of his department, this year, there is an appropriation of $10,973,548, that is, more than $8,500,000 is set apart exclusively for military purposes and almost $2,500,000 for the navy.
In a country like Canada where the national debt increases by hundreds of millions of dollars, I contend that it is more than time to cut out military expenditure. The budget of that department is equivalent to one dollar per capita of the population. More than $260,000 are expended on the League of Nations so as to foster disarmament, while, on the other

The Budget-Mr. Rheaume
hand, millions of dollars are expended for military purposes. The administration of this department alone amounts to $320,000, the cadet service $100,000, contingencies $35,000, engineering service $327,500, general stores $063,500, non-permanent active militia $1,837,-400-namely $168,600 less than last year.
I am, sir, fairly well informed on this nonpermanent active militia. In the appropriation pertaining to this matter are included the following items, service, maintenance, pay and allowances with reference to the administration, the training of the militia in camps, staffs, in schools of instruction, target practice, grants to associations, etc. I state that there is no greater waste of money in this country than that which is expended on military training camps. I know of what I am talking about as we have almost every year such camps in the town of St. John's and this has been so for a great number of years past. The town is invaded by regiments of 600, 700, 800 men more or less, who have no knowledge whatsoever of military training, they cannot handle a rifle or understand a word of English. They are fitted up indifferently and come over to this training camp for two weeks, at the country's expense. Millions of dollars are wasted in giving officers the opportunity of taking holidays, at the state's expense. In a poor country like ours, during a crisis, when people are starving, I state that these millions of dollars should be applied to help the unemployed and the needy.
In the item of $4,844,000 appropriated to permanent troops, there is a decrease of $206,000. I have already expressed my views as regards military schools and permanent troops. There exists such a military school in the town of St. John's. I do not wish to express an opinion whether it is better or worse than the others. I am certain that the officers and men of this school follow the same regulations as others established in this country. A few hours per day are devoted to training so as to raise an appetite, and all this at the government's expense. .The country meanwhile is millions of dollars in debt. I contend that it is more than time to forego such waste of money. I note that the Royal Military College will cost this year $360,500, namely, a decrease of $25,500. If I be not mistaken, in order to enter this college, one must be well off. If the government wished to put into practice what they advocate, they should first replace these military colleges by agricultural schools.
The government has asked this house for a blank signature so as to dispose of unlimited amounts for unemployment and farm relief.
Let them do away with military schools and replace them by agricultural schools and thus make of our sons good farmers and citizens.
The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) stated this week that the future of Canada depended on farming. I have in hand the budget of agriculture for 1932-33. As I stated just now the population of Canada reaches 10,000,000 and the expenditure per capita for farming is sixty cents, while it amounts to more than one dollar for the militia. In 1931-1932, the estimates of agriculture amounted to $9,929,000; this year they are only $6,671,000, a decrease of $3,258,000. I wonder why our friends opposite, who represent rural counties, and especially those from the west who represent essentially farming constituencies, tolerate a cut of $3,000,000 in the agricultural estimates, while only a cut of $1,302,000 for the National Defence and $1,606,000 for the naval service, is made. I state, sir, that it has no sense. My views are that the militia budget should be cut by 75 per cent and that of Agriculture increased proportionately.
The experimental farms' appropriations are decreased this year by $833,000, while those of the Royal Military College at Kingston are only reduced $25,500, a difference of $808,000. And the government is bold enough to state that it is to relieve the farmers that a blank signature is requested! I trust that the people of this country will open their eyes and see which of the two parties is the champion of the farmers. I note that the grants for agricultural exhibitions are cut down S300,000, that for dairy industry $63,700, for the health of cattle and inspection of meat $896,000, almost a million. What care are they taking of the health of the citizens of this country?
Some hon. MEMBERS (Translation): Hear, hear.

After
slaughtering cattle infected with tuberculosis, the amount appropriated for that purpose is reduced by $896,000, while the estimates affected to the non-permanent troops is only cut down $168,600. One must keep within reasonable limits. It is quite proper to support a political party, however one must preserve some common sense. One must not forget that members represent the electorate of their constituency. I spy the hon. member for Berthier (Mr. Barrette), the hon. member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Lafleche) who represent two beautiful farming counties as fine as mine-*
Mr. BARRETTE (Translation); Finer.

Perhaps so. When we are aware of decreases such, for instance as that of $376,700 in the appropriation for the administration of the Destructive Insect and Pest Act, while a cut of only $206,000 is made on the permanent militia, I state that one must keep within reasonable limits-I see that the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins), is in his seat, he is the champion of live stock. I am aware that he has the rank of a colonel; perhaps, military matters are of a greater concern to him than agriculture or live stock. I wonder what he thinks of the $150,000 cut in the live stock appropriation.
The estimates intended for publications which the government distribute throughout the country to help the farmers-and which deal with the work carried on at the various experimental farms-are reduced by $30,500, while militia contingencies are larger than that amount.

I am simply commenting on the present budget.
Some hon. MEMBERS (Translation): Hear, hear!

I notice in the budget that an expenditure of $20,000,000 was made in the western provinces. In no way do I feel envious, far be it from my thoughts; I am aware that the west is in dire circumstances; we have there compatriots and we must help them out. I regret that the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull) is not in his seat, because I should have given him a message for the Prime Minister of his province. I shall ask his good Conservative friends who represent farming constituencies to endeavour to obtain a two cents per pound bonus on butter.
That was Mr. Houde's policy which you cried down in the last Quebec provincial election.
All are aware that the price of butter has come down to 18 cents per pound within the last few days, to-morrow it may perhaps reach 16 cents.
Is that your wish?
No, sir, we want the government to give a bonus on butter just as they did on western wheat.
There will be one.
The hon. Postmaster General promised one at the last provincial election.
We shall see that he keeps his pledge!

I want to give you some idea of the prices of farm products. If I request a rebate, a direct aid for the eastern provinces, it is because of their precarious financial situation. Many of them have failed within the last few months and if business does not improve within the next six months, I think that there will be thousands of farmers who will fail in the eastern provinces. Wholesale butter, last week, sold at IS cents; eggs retailed at IS cents a dozen; potatoes 40 cents per bag; pork $6.50 per cwt., beef 5 cents per pound, veal 4 cents per pound; cow hides, 2, 3 and 4 cents, calf hides, 4 and 5 cents, country hides, 35 cents a piece.
I listened to our friends opposite state that from 1921 to 1930, we had had a. bad regime which had ruined the country. I would ask them to compare the prices of to-day with those of 1921 to 1930.
What do you designate country hides?

Country hides, sir, are the hides of calves which the farmers slaughter themselves and sell in the village or to a leather dealer; it is what we call "a farmer's hide" and is not supposed to be worth as much as a hide which comes from the Montreal slaughter-houses or city butchers.
Now, sir, I wish to make a few comments on the luxury tax. I regret that the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) is not in his seat, however, I trust that his good friend, the hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sutherland), will draw his attention to my remarks or that he will read them in Hansard. This luxury tax was discontinued, I do not know by whom, however, if an error was

The Budget-Mr. Rheaume
committed, it is when this luxury tax was abolished, and this to the detriment of the people. The following are a few comparisons: a golf suit costs $25; this is about the same price as a workman's Sunday suit, and the tax is the same in both instances; dress suits and tuxedos, etc., are taxed the same amount as for an ordinary man's winter coat. As for ladies' evening dresses, well, I have a wife and daughters, so I know what they cost. I am not opposed to wealth, on the contrary; however, one must draw a line between necessities and luxury. One purchases an evening dress for $40, $50, $60 and $75 and yet you pay the same tax as when you purchase a decent or comfortable coat for your wife. If a man has the means to purchase an evening dress for $60 or $75, so that his wife may attend a ball or an evening party, this gentleman can certainly afford to pay 10 per cent of a luxury tax and hand over $6 or S7 to the state which certainly needs the revenue.
I shall now, sir, draw your attention to a few articles pertaining to sport, not that I disapprove of sports. Perhaps one will say that I am not a golf player, it is true; however, I am a member of a golf club and of many other clubs, and I like sports. Even this morning, I noticed in a store window on Rideau street, golf shoes selling at $2.50, $4, $5, $6 and even $9. When a person can purchase a pair of shoes for $2.50 and he prefers to purchase a pair for $9, surely there must be an average price that might serve as a^ basis. A person who can afford $5, $6 or $7 more for a pair of shoes, can certainly pay a luxury tax of 50 or 60 cents. I saw some quite nice golf stick bags for $3 50-there were others for $12.50; these articles sold at five different prices. An average price could be fixed. One who purchases a $12.50 article for a golf stick bag when he can purchase one for S3.50, should pay a luxury tax on the difference. I also noticed that golf sticks were on sale at prices ranging from $2.50 to $6. The sales tax on a golf stick is the same as on a pick or shovel. Tennis rackets were marked $2, $4, $6, $8, $10, up to $18. I am in favour of encouraging sports, however, I contend that when a person can purchase a tennis racket for $2, $4, $5 or $6, and that person pays $18, he can afford paying 10 per cent more to help his country.
You will not be looked upon as a sport.

The same tax is levied on automobiles "de luxe" as that
which is paid by a poor person who purchases a motor truck to earn a livelihood or a salesman who needs a car to earn his living.
There is an article of first necessity which has somewhat drawn my attention, namely matches. They are sold three boxes for 25 cents. There is a sales tax of i a cent and an excise tax of 3 cents per box. If you purchase twelve boxes worth $1, you pay 6 cents according to the new sales tax and 36 cents of excise tax, which means 52 cents tax on $1. Now if you purchase a box of chocolates of $1, there is no apparent tax. Would it not be fairer to levy this luxury or excise tax on the box of chocolates than on an article of first necessity as are matches? When you pay $1 for a box of chocolates, so as to satisfy your greediness, I state that this is a luxury. I wonder, sir, if the famous budget so much praised yesterday really meets with the approval of the people?

Hear,
hear!
I shall now refer to what is known as a grandfather's clock. I had the occasion, together with a group of friends, of purchasing one so as to make a present. The prices ranged from $150 to $600.
That was a ''de luxe" present!

I state that a person who purchases a grandfather's clock for $600 when one can be purchased for $150 or $200, can afford paying a luxury tax of 10 per cent.
I now come to dining-room sets. Last week, I saw in a large Montreal store a dining-room set priced at $1,200.

Hear,
hear!

I understand that quite a heavy duty is levied on furniture. A nice dining-room set can be purchased, to-day, for 8200 or $300, however if a person pays $1,200, to satisfy a whim or to boast of the finest dining-room set in the town or village, that person can certainly afford to contribute something to the exchequer.
I further wish to refer to articles considered a luxury such as diamonds, rings, etc. I am not opposed to jewels. Whether a person buys, in Montreal, Ottawa or anywhere, jewels to please some lady, no objection can be

taken. Last week, I saw at Birks, in Montreal, a diamond worth $2,500. I contend that if a person can afford purchasing a diamond ring, either for himself or as a gift to his wife or his girl. . .
She must be very pretty 1

It matters little; however; I state that such a person can afford paying a tax on articles considered a luxury especially, when a tax of 42 per cent is levied on matches. The hon. Minister of Finance is in his seat. I trust that in his next budget-unless he wishes to amend this one-he will consider levying a tax on luxuries.
I shall not add anything further, as I know that a number of my colleagues wish to take part in this debate. The country made a mistake two years ago, it knows it now, and awaits its opportunity.
The Liberal party brought prosperity to this country from 1896 to 1911. From 1911 to 1914 prosperity left u&. I do not think that the Conservative party can blame it on their ill luck, but rather on their bad administration. I inquired from a number of old politicians and none remembered that the Conservative party had ever had a surplus in any year. I shall not refer to the period between 1914 and 1918, it was during the war, neither to the years between 1918 and 1921. The Liberal party assumed power in 1921. During two years it had to put up with deficits, however, after balancing the budget, from 1923 to 1930, there were surpluses every year, the national debt was decreased and the country entered an era of prosperity.
Of bankruptcy.
You are in error.
You are responsible for this bankruptcy.

From 1923 to 1930, we were blessed with surpluses. Look at the trade we carried on with other countries. I notice the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge is all ears, I wish to thank him, I am aware that he is well-read, clear-headed and I hope in days to come, will be appointed to the Senate.
Some hon. MEMBERS (Translation): Hear, hear!
Incidentally, I state that if his party appoint him, it will be as a tribute for his services to the party.

Many
thanks!

As I mentioned a few moments ago, from 1921 to 1930, Canada was prosperous. We traded with foreign countries. It is by doing a good business that a person amasses wealth; however, from 1930 to this day, we have been losing ground. I realize that the Conservative party will reply: the world is undergoing a crisis. In 1930, we also stated that unemployment in Canada was not due to a poor administration but rather to a world wide crisis. My opponent in the election stated: place the Conservative party in power and we pledge ourselves to bring back prosperity in this country within two months.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to add anything further, however, I feel certain that at the next general election, the people will choose the party which has always given protection to the farmer and workmen, because if the people were prosperous and happy, it was certainly under the Liberal regime from 1921 to
1930.

Mr. Speaker, I agree with everything
the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie) said with regard to the effect on the morale of our people of lipsticks, rubber tires and salacious literature. I am sorry I was unable to follow the remarks of the hon. member who just took his seat, buit the French language is very beautiful, and if, when it has been translated, the speech of the hon. gentleman reads as it sounded to me, I am sure it will be very fine indeed. I understand that the Acting Speaker (Mr. Sullivan) himself speaks very beautiful French, and my neighbour intimated to me that the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat took advantage of the temporary position of the hon. member for St. Ann (Mr. Sullivan) to mention something he said yesterday in a speech which was equally effective. I greatly appreciated the humorous, inoffensive and clever manner in which the Acting Speaker was cornered.
The question has often been asked as to what extent the present crisis is due to the world situation and to what extent it has been caused by the lack of an internal policy. I hope the Minister of Finance will excuse me

The Budget-Mr. Luchkovich
if I do not deal specifically with the budget; my purpose to-day is to discuss the problem from a universal and particularly an European standpoint, and I hope at some other opportune time to deal with the internal aspect of this subject.
One of the most profound impressions an observant traveller in Europe must bring back with him is a realization of the interdependence of the nations and the absolute necessity for greater cooperation among all the countries of the world if we are to enjoy some semblance of the prosperity of the past two decades, and in order to obtain this cooperation the obstacles that stand in the way first must be removed.
The world is clamouring for peace, but there is no peace; it wants a return of prosperity, but there is no prosperity, for we cannot attain the latter without a propagation and realization of the former. We cannot eat our cake and at the same time have it. Briefly, it is the old story of the futility of trying to make an omelette without breaking an egg, the folly of attempting to maintain peace without an application of the essential contributory conditions, and the impossibility of a return of prosperity without the cultivation of the necessary peaceful arts and pursuits incidental thereto. At no time has the truth of the situation been brought home with greater force than during the past few years of financial stringency and economic chaos. More and more clearly are people beginning to realize the uniform character of the world and the utter impossibility, in this great age of industrial development, of any country living unto itself. Thus such phrases as "self-contained nation," "splendid isolation," are rapidly becoming obsolete and devoid of meaning, and even the famous admonition of George Washington against any foreign entanglements seems likely to be discarded as an outworn political anachronism; for the United States is just as involved in world affairs as any other nation and her future is just as dependent upon a successful solution of universal economic problems as that of any other country. In other words, she can no longer live apart from the rest of the world and retain her relative position therein, but she must unite with the other nations to restore the proper balance and stability essential to a return to prosperity.
As regards Canada and the United States our troubles can be traced directly back to Europe where present conditions have for the most part originated. It seems strange that the richest country in the world, with all her
vaunted wealth and great hoards of gold should, notwithstanding, have one of the largest armies of unemployment in the world. But such being the case, it can be attributed to no other cause than that the economic unity of the universe has in some manner been disturbed. For immediate causes one must refer to the lack of purchasing power on the part of people overseas. If Europe cannot buy, America cannot sell. For many decades the European market has absorbed the surplus products of this continent, such as wheat, meat, cotton, oil and many highly finished manufactures, but of late years the accumulating bankruptcy consequent upon the great war has left Europe so weak and impoverished as to make impossible of maintenance anything like the trade European countries used to call for in pre-war days. Matters have reached such a pass that our neighbour's troubles merge with our own difficulties on this and the other side of the ocean and that ours cannot be solved without a simultaneous solution of theirs.
My travels led me through some of the northern and central parts of the European continent, comprising a long, continuously changing panorama of formerly bustling urban activity, majestic mountain grandeur and exquisite pastoral beauty and simplicity, and during the entire extent of the journey the sun had shone down on all this beautiful scenery in a veritable blaze of glory, creating in one a momentary impression that all was right with the world and that this glorious sunshine and the products drawn by its power out of the rich European soil were ever at the undisturbed disposal of the inhabitants and possessors thereof. It was not until I had spoken to the peoples in the different countries I had visited and had been shown various ruins and wrecks, many evidences of which could be seen all over Europe, that the other side of the picture began to unfold itself. These ruins and the consequent industrial stagnation of the war broke every delusion I had about that continent in spite of its great culture, history, traditions and scenic appeal. I had thought that the devastating character of the last great war would forevermore become an object lesson to the belligerent countries, but their hatred and suspicion of each other have increased rather than decreased since the world war. I believe the fault lies in the system under which Europeans have been brought up rather than in the people themselves who, in my opinion, have become merely the victims of a vicious war

The Budget-Mr. Luchkovich
psychology or propaganda. Propaganda may have had a very doubtful value during the throes of war, but in time of peace it is inconceivable how hate, blindness and error are allowed to stifle the natural impulse of man to seek the truth and live in harmony with his fellows.
Before my departure as the Canadian delegate to the Interparliamentary Union at Bucharest, I had entertained a somewhat hazy attitude toward the question of disarmament; but when, during the course of my journey I found out how alike are all the- peoples of the world, how similar their cares, joys, longings, lives and ambitions, and when I realized how universal are the decency, honesty and worthiness of the common man, I frankly admit I felt no pangs of conscience in voting against a proposed resolution to set up an armed force for the League of Nations as well as against other motions that I thought might perpetuate the damnable war spirit that had separated Europe into so many factions and that has prevented her from regaining her strength and taking her proper position in the world. I could not help contemplating the part that Canada should and must play in the ever-changing scheme of world affairs, for ever since I was a young man playing baseball on the sand lots of my little coal-mining birthplace with .contemporaries of a multitude of racial origin, my mind has been deeply agitated over the great common heritage given to us on this side of the ocean by a Supreme Being to .perpetuate the old and yet new doctrine of peace, good-will and the brotherhood of man. Notwithstanding the vicissitudes, exigencies and antipathies resulting from a peculiar psychology of racial warfare, I nevertheless still retain the hope and optimism bom of the democracy of youthful experiences, that Canada will some day become, as it were, a beacon light, to the rest of the world, tom by bitter strife and racial animosities to show the way to a more complete and mutual understanding amongst the various constituent elements thereof. In order to get a good picture of Europe hon. members should visualize a continent much smaller in size than Canada but with about forty times our papulation, and composed of some thirty sovereign states, each with its own army, its central government, its frontiers and the usual customs barriers, differing in race and religion, and with all the smouldering feuds and antagonisms of by-gone centuries. This seething, restless conglomeration of races-where did they all originate? Where did they come from; what were their sorrows, their joys and their ambitions? Those were questions, Mr. Speaker, which I put to

myself and found exceedingly fascinating. Taking them individually I found some very charming, cultured and progressive individuals, but judging them as nations I had seen and heard only too much of the mutual hatred and distrust which has persisted in Europe so bitterly all down through the ages. When I had finally completed my journey and found myself on board ship again quietly contemplating the whole situation, I could not help but draw a parallel with our own' miniature Europe in Canada, and note the difference in attitude on the part of our polyglot and cosmopolitan races which are making their contribution to the building up of this great nation-difference in attitude not only towards each other tout also towards the country of their adoption; and I thought, Mr. Speaker, that if something of the tolerance and good will, something of the spirit of friendship and mutual cooperation which characterize our various peoples in this country in meeting their problems could only be infused into their kinsmen on the other side of the Atlantic ocean there would not have been any occasion for the huge burdens of debts and for the nervous piling up of armaments which slowly but surely must bring about the collapse and ruin of every country in Europe.
It is true that we on this side of the ocean have a crisis also, but I think that that is largely due to the breakdown of our foreign markets. Europe has always absorbed our exportable surplus of wheat and other grains, and therefore I think it is the resurrection of that market that will bring about a revival of trade and the return of prosperity in this country. This, of course, does not ignore the existence of our vast internal problems which call for immediate solution, or the necessity of setting our own house in order so that we may adjust ourselves more effectively to world conditions.
In stressing the European situation, Mr. Speaker, I am seeking no alibi for our lack of a policy in this country. My purpose is merely to call attention to the basic unity of the world in which no country can live unto itself, and where each is dependent on the other to the extent of its own deficiencies as well as the others' ability to supply and our own ability to pay. Someone in this country has said that all trade is essentially barter and that commodities can only be paid for in goods. I was very much surprised to learn while over in England that out of the 175 million bushels of wheat which they annually import into that country, 105 million bushels come from foreign sources, while only

Just how much this disproportion is due to Canada's unwillingness to buy more British goods I am at the moment unable to say, but I feel confident that if our volume of imports from the British Isles was increased it would react most favourably on our export trade in wheat and other food products, for it is hard to understand how Canada and the mother country can trade other than on a reciprocal basis. Only the other day the Right Hon. Mr. Thomas in England made this statement:
Canada may say, we are interested mainly in wheat, and from the standpoint of Great Britain the most important and indeed the only factor is what they will do in regard to our manufactures.
In plain English that means: If you want us to buy more of your wheat, you must buy more of our manufactures. When Mr. Thomas specifically referred to wheat in regard to Canada's trade with Great Britain he evidently must have been aware of the predominance of wheat as our staple export. Indeed so extensive has our grain trade become that from a country trading originally in only fish, fur and lumber, the sale of our grain in foreign markets has within the past three decades taken precedence over all other products in Canada. In 1932 nearly forty per cent of our total exports, valued at nearly half a billion dollars, was grain products. Indeed, it is through the grain trade that Canada reached the peak of her prosperity, and it is through that trade that she must regain it; for our foreign trade is the lifestream and foundation of our economic structure, and any restriction or curtailment thereof must strike directly and most powerfully upon the primary producers of this country, whose very existence depends upon a profitable sale of their products in markets abroad. Under the circumstances farmers cannot continue indefinitely to sell their products under the cost of production and at the same time maintain a fair and decent standard of living and meet all their various obligations. This condition has its limitations, and unless some methods of enlarging our markets and improving the system of distribution of our products to those markets are evolved, agriculture in the west is likely to sink into hopeless insolvency from which it may never recover, and when a basic industry like farming fails it is bound to affect adversely every other industry in Canada.
I had intended, Mr. Speaker, to say a few words aibout the tariff, but the tariff as one of the disturbing factors in trade recovery has been so thoroughly discussed that I think it
would ibe superfluous for me to rehash the old stereotyped arguments here this afternoon. It may, however, serve some useful purpose to point out the utter futility of economic tariff warfare not only in solving our internal problems in Canada but also in stabilizing world conditions. Tariff revision is a world problem, and as such must be solved by the world at large. I do not think it can be accomplished by unilateral agreement ; it must be accomplished by the mutual consent and cooperation of all the countries simultaneously, to do any real or genuine good.
During my visit to Europe I could not help but feel that the continent was too top heavy to last very long without collapsing, and that only an economic union of all the states thereof could save it from ultimate ruin. An American editor has said:
The way to understand Europe's economic tangle is to picture Canada as if it were [DOT] hacked and divided by customs and military barriers, so that goods, from Vancouver to Montreal would be inspected and charged duty at every few miles.
Such duplication of governmental, military and administrative machinery would be far more than Canada could bear, and it is certainly a load which Europe cannot carry either at the present or any time in the future. Among other obstacles to a return of world prosperity are disarmament, a settlement of the problems of international indebtedness, and the question of minorities. The Versailles treaty was supposed to set the European house in order, but it seems rather to have left a couple of ghosts which appear at frequent intervals to haunt the makers of the treaty and destroy their peace of mind. Senator Borah, chairman of the United States foreign affairs committee, wants to revise the treaty, and so do many others. He comes out flat-footed on the debt question and asks that war reparations and war debts be cancelled. On top of all this, sir, the minorities in Europe are clamouring in ever-accumulating zeal for autonomous freedom within their own ethnographical boundaries or else complete absorption within their own racial groups. On the other hand, so intent are the newly set up states in Europe in hammering together the various constituent elements thereof into one homogeneous whole, foy riding roughshod over their minorities, that little heed is paid to the cry of self-determination or to the minority treaties which have been placed under the guarantee of the League of Nations, and by which most of the post-war countries in Europe are bound.

I never saw so many soldiers in all my life as I did on my trip across the European continent. All along the railway lines one could see numerous sentries on guard. Here and there regiments of new recruits were being drilled, and in the restaurants, theatres and railway trains it seemed as if the well-groomed officers were the only patrons. It was not until one encountered the abject poverty of the cities, towns and rural districts that the sight of these well-fed officers became extremely ominous and significant. Time after time the picture of Canada with her 4,000 miles of unpatrolled boundary line, and her very meagre force of men under arms, came to my mind, and I could not help but feel a little homesick for the country where armaments were almost negligible and where war occupied the smallest place in our thoughts. The horrible vision of beautiful glorious Europe poverty stricken on the one hand and soldier infested on the other will always remain an object lesson to me of the folly of maintaining militarism and at the same time hoping for a return of prosperity. Such a futile hope, Mr. Speaker, can only end in despair; for much as the nations would like to disarm, they dare not because of fear of their neighbours, which has grown, rather than diminished, since the last great war. After thirteen years of peace there are now more men under arms than in 1914. Little wonder, therefore, is it that the nations hover so dangerously on the verge of bankruptcy and complete collapse.
In addition to the costs of armaments Europe is shackled by huge war and other debts. I do not think it worth while to mention the amount of those debts, because hon. members are familiar with the figures. British opinion is in favour of wiping out completely all war debts, and is sincere in its desire for a greater industrial prosperity in Germany. But the revival of a strong, industrially prosperous Germany relieved of crushing war debts will hardly be accepted in a friendly spirit by France, whose whole policy in regard to Germany has been based on overwhelming fear, and the consequent determination to keep this neighbouring country down; but how long Germany can be kept down, or how long the German nation can be suppressed without pulling the rest of Europe down, including France, remains to be seen. So far as I am concerned nations of the world cannot get together too soon to eradicate the evils which brought about and continue to sustain the present depression. I have always been puzzled to know why the minorities question has been so ignored, 
and yet it is one of the main factors of the present chaos and dissension in Europe. Nations cannot be dismembered without leaving behind a lot of ill feeling and a sense of injustice. From what I saw of the rankling bitterness caused by the revision of the map of Europe I cannot help but feel that a little revision here and there would do much towards restoring a better and more harmonious balance. Love of one's country and one's race is a powerful source of many virtues and acts of heroism when it is based on and controlled by ethical laws. When it degenerates, however, into immoderate nationalism it soon becomes a source of countless acts of injustice and wrong. Look at the situation in Europe to-day. Forty million people have been cut off from their ethnical and racial groups by the Versailles treaty. They are being subjected to unspeakable outrages in the name of chauvinistic nationalism. So intent are these new post-war countries upon obliterating all traces of the diversity of the races within their borders that little attention is paid to the stipulations and provisions by which these countries are bound in respect of the minorities. When one therefore realizes that all these atrocities are committed in spite of the fact that minority rights are guaranteed by the League of Nations, and that most of these minorities live in close contiguity to strong kindred nations, the remark made by a certain writer, that Europe is sitting on a volcano which might at any moment erupt and light a flame throughout the world, is based as much on the minorities question as it is on any other of the problems that are harassing the world to-day.
In regard to the race question in Europe, one must take into account the fact that we are dealing with conditions and not theories, concrete situations and not abstract unrealities; for much as one might wish to warp existent realities to suit preconceived ideas of what should or should not be done, one cannot afford to ignore the human element, the peculiar innate characteristic pride, aspirations and ambitions that so stubbornly persist in all races and make people and conditions just what they are. Nothing keeps extreme nationalism alive like the forcible suppression of nationalism. If hon. members could only visualize the hopeless despair of suppressed desire, the cruel pain of thwarted effort, and the spiritual hell resultant therefrom, it would enable them to realize more clearly not only the tragedy but also the great injustice of the situation. Each race feels it is just as good as the other, and it is extremely galling to their self-respect to live in continual physical and

The Budget-Mr. Picket
spiritual subjugation and forced negation of the very qualities which the superpossessed races consider a virtue in themselves but a sin in those who unfortunately find themselves under their domination. But races somehow will not stay down; and as history has given us countless examples of the folly of forcible suppression, nothing less than a grant of autonomy and liberty of cultural development will free Europe from one of its potential menaces to peace and well-being.
The achievement of self-determination may after all be necessary in order to attain fuller growth and a wider conception of responsibilities. Their pride satisfied, the races should thus be unimpeded in their progressive march to a better civilization. At the present time the minorities in Europe are more interested in political than economic liberation; but once the former- is attained they ought to be able to devote their undivided attention to the latter problem. In any case civilization is not a standard but a continuous creative process requiring two simultaneous cooperative impulsions,-that which consists of the fulfilment of a common desire and that which comprises a pooling of separate individual contributions. The tendency of races is, primarily, to develop as separate entities, and secondarily, as parts of one cosmos or united universe. Although probably too much emphasis is being laid on the former and too little on the latter, I do not think that there is anything inconsistent in advocating cultural freedom, or even self-determination, of the races and the economic unity of the world at the same time. Such unity is impossible without peace, and peace is hardly likely unless justice is done to the forty million minorities in Europe.
Many centuries ago a great writer said:
In necessariis uni-tas, in du'biis libertas, in omnibus caritas-essentials unity, in doubtful matters liberty, in all things charity.
Those wise words, Mr. Speaker, may well be applied to the situation in Europe. Economic unity is very essential, and it is a matter on which all the nations of the world should place a great deal of emphasis. I do not think we can have prosperity in Canada unless we have prosperity in Europe. It is true that we have questions on this side of the ocean which call for immediate attention, but nevertheless I believe that unless the situation in Europe is changed it is hardly likely we shall have immediate prosperity in this country.

I wish to extend to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) my congratulations on his excellent presentation of the budget. I liked the manner of its delivery and particularly the absence of partisanship throughout the whole speech.
From the capitalistic point of view undoubtedly this is a good budget; that is, if we are to continue putting the interests of capital above the welfare of human beings. But since that is not my idea, it does not seem to me to be a good budget, particularly in the methods relied on for raising taxes. For the most part the new taxes are to be levied on the great masses of the people; the consumers will have to pay them. It is true the income tax will be paid by those

on whom it is levied, but the sales tax, the nuisance taxes and the excise tax-which seems to be a new name for a tariff tax-are passed on to the consuming masses. This will increase unemployment, because the purchasing power of the people will be still further reduced, and at the moment it is dangerously low. So I do not favour the minister's method of raising revenue.
I should like to see the income tax very much increased, but not on the lower incomes; instead of an increase of one hundred per cent in the income tax on a $4,000 income, and reducing this percentage until on an income of $100,000 the increase is only thirty-two per cent, I would graduate the increased percentage the other way, so that the higher the income the higher would be the rate of income tax. I think very soon the time will come when we shall levy taxes on those who have the money to pay them. I have said that before in this house, and I shall continue to say so until finally it will be done. Really the masses of the people, our workingmen and farmers, are not able to carry any greater tax burden than that under which they are at present staggering. As a matter of fact, many of them are not able to pay their present taxes.
I was interested in the proposal made on Tuesday by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) that the state should take over all incomes in excess of $25,000. Why not? At the present time we are in a jam because we have a surplus of goods, but those goods cannot be bought by the people who need them. There are persons enjoying large incomes who could spend more, but they aTe satisfying all their needs. In fact they do not know how to spend their money. The only way in which they spend it is in creating more machinery to produce more goods to add to the present surplus. Really it would be a convenience to them to suggest another channel of expenditure. True, they snap up government bonds, as we found out this year when the government floated certain loans; those loans were oversubscribed by people with more money than they knew what to do with. But we need a great deal of money to run this country, and by taking it from the masses in the form of burdensome taxation we are simply causing a greater amount of unemployment. Therefore it seems to mo that it would be the part of wisdom-although I know that it does not sound sane in this house-to take over this accumulated wealth for the benefit of the state. Indeed, this would not be a very great hardship to our wealthy people, because their wealth will not

Not only am I in favour of increasing the income tax on the larger incomes, but I am also in favour of an inheritance tax. Really I do not see why money should be inherited in such vast amounts. You cannot inherit education, you cannot inherit any accomplishment. When great sums of money are passed from generation to generation it really means that children yet unborn are destined to become the slaves Qf other children yet unborn, who by reason of the wealth they inherit from their parents will be able to command the services of hundreds of thousands of people. These whose services are commanded have not a chance to start life on even terms with their more favoured fellow citizens. I have in my hand what has been quoted in this house before, but I do not think it can be quoted too often. It is said that in the United States in 1929 five hundred and four persons had an aggregate net income equal to the gross amount paid to one million and thirty-two thousand cotton farmers and one million three hundred thousand wheat farmers. That condition of things cannot be justified. It is wholly immoral. It is just a question of how long it will take our people-because a similar situation exists in this country-the masses of our people, our workmen, farmers and small business men, to realize what this means, and to see to it that this great wealth shall be conscripted and applied to social uses to relieve the toiling masses from the burden of taxation that is driving them to desperation. Apparently the time is not yet ripe for this to be done, but it will be done, either during this depression or when we are in another, but in any case it will not be very long before in this intelligent age we shall see to it that those who have amassed great wealth by some means or other, legal but immoral, disgorge that wealth to take care of the social necessities of our people.
With respect to the Imperial economic conference that is to be held in this city in July, I have this to say to the government, although I know' it does not matter whether I say it or not. They v'ould be very wise not to parade the Imperial conference as much as they have done; at any rate I would suggest that they do not parade it any more, because the more people expect from it the worse it is going to be-for the government. I do not for one moment think that the Imperial conference is going to be the world-shaking event that we have been led to think. As a matter of fact, I agree with the hon. member for St. Ann (Mr. Sullivan), who spoke the other night.
I will quote his exact words because they say just about what I want to say in this regard. The hon. gentleman said:
The Imperial conference will sit in Ottav'a in the month of July.
I think that is about what they will do; and for their sake I pray that it will not be as hot as it was last July, for that would be a bit hard on the old country people. Let us consider the Imperial conference for a moment. It is not that I do not want it to succeed; I do want it to succeed. But how can it? Last year the Canadian Prime Minister went over to Great Britain to tell the British people what they should do. They were to put up a tariff around Britain and give us a preference inside, while in return we were to leave the tariff against Britain where it was but raise the tariff against other countries ten per cent. In brief, Canada said to Britain, "You buy our goods and in return we won't buy yours." Since that time we have artificially jacked up in three ways the prices of British goods coming to Canada by artificially stabilizing the pound; by juggling with the value of goods for customs purposes; and by the new-fangled tariff called the excise. In other words, three times since then we have said to Britain, "We want you to buy from us but we don't want to buy from you."
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), in his very excellent speech the other night, a speech that interested me greatly up to a point and then disappointed me terribly, talked about the things he would like to get from the British Empire. I have all the articles mentioned, but rubber was one of them-things that are coming in free; we shall get these from other parts of the empire. I fancy that will not interest the industrialists of Great Britain very much; at any rate it does not seem to me to be a major concession.
This is the thing that we must realize, and I think we all do realize it, and we might as well admit it, namely, that Canada's trade with the empire has been declining. In the calendar year 1931 we bought 75.S per cent of our imports and sold 63.6 per cent of our exports outside the British Empire. In 1914 the empire took 55.3 per cent of our exports and in 1929 only 39.3 per cent. But the share of our trade with the United States, both exports and imports, has remained fairly constant over -the same period, in spite of American and Canadian tariffs. As a matter of fact Canadian trade has expanded more with "other foreign countries" other than the United States. It is with these countries that

we have made our greatest increase in selling and buying. From 1914 to 1929 our exports to "other foreign countries" increased from 7 per cent to 24 per cent, representing almost one-quarter of the total trade. I am using figures from the Canadian Forum compiled by "F.H.U." who is Professor Underhill, I think. But there is something else to notice:
Our greatest group of export commodities consists of wheat and wheat flour. We grow so much wheat in Canada that Great Britain cannot possibly absorb it all, and we are therefore dependent upon world markets. Our second greatest group of export commodities consists of forest products, lumber, shingles, pulpwood, pulp and paper, and for these the United States is the greatest market. Even if Great Britain shuts out the Scandinavian countries and the wicked Russians, her market, as Professor Underhill says, cannot be a substitute for the American market which we already have.
In view of all these facts, which are known to all of us, it is foolish to hope that -we shall be able to -build up empire trade unless each part of the empire makes concessions to the others. This is the thing which the government ought to take to heart: It cannot be done with -the attitude which the government took in Great Britain last year and which they have held consistently since. Unless we are willing to buy goods from Great Britain, we cannot expect her to go on buying in large quantities from us. Personally, therefore, I do not think that the Imperial conference, which, as the hon. member for St. Ann so aptly said the other night, is to sit in Ottawa in July, will be a great success. I do not think it can be.
