away back in 1930 that the farmer was becoming discouraged, you can take "becoming" out and say that the farmer is discouraged. It seems to me that the government which is now in power will have to embark upon a policy of inflation, because when the farmers of Canada send their products, we will say, to England, and are paid in English money, when they get that translated into Canadian currency, they receive less for their product than it actually brought in Liverpool, little as that was. I do not see how we can go on doing this, and so finally we shall go into a policy of inflation, or "reflation," or whatever you like to call it. I do not care what the term is, but there simply must come about a closer relationship between the amount of goods to be moved and the amount of money in circulation. I believe we shall have to acquire a new idea of money and think of money as something that transports goods from the person who sells them to the person who needs them, and then the services that money performs can be paid for. But we are not now over paying for the services it performs; we are paying tremendous wages to money for services which, as it happens, it does not perform.
I feel very keenly in regard to the agricultural situation, and I think hon. members can readily understand why. It is not simply that I represent an agricultural constituency; it is that these men and women, boys and girls, are the best we have in Canada. Remember this, that agricultural people are the source not only of our food supply but of our national life, and if we cannot keep on the farm a decent standard, not only economic but cultural; if we cannot hold our best blood on the land, at least as the source of the life of our urban centres, then indeed, we shall be sapping our national life at its very source.
I have always been extremely interested in cooperative endeavours. I have felt for a long time that farmers can do very much to make their life better by selling, processing and completely marketing their own products cooperatively and buying cooperatively what they need; but you cannot successfully build up cooperative enterprises on a falling commodity price level; it simply cannot be done. If you can keep your price level steady, or if you have a price level that is rising, then the building up of cooperative enterprises is an easy matter, but if you try to build up a cooperative enterprise on a falling market all you do is to bring one more cooperative concern to an end and to discredit the whole movement. For instance, last year we had a
number of wise people in the house who knew how the pools got into difficulties. The reason was simply that the price of wheat fell to almost nothing. We have a little abattoir up at Barrie, the first thing of its kind in Ontario. It is experimental; we are trying to have the farmer process his own hogs, lambs and calves. What happened? Three things. First of all, the government pays high interest rates, and so all other enterprises in Canada must do the same thing. Secondly, there was a falling commodity price level, which meant that the meat that you put in to cure was put in at a price higher than that at which it could be sold when they came out of cure, and of course you cannot make money fast that way. Thirdly, in Canada we lack efficient trained men with social consciousness. You can hardly find them. There are some, I am glad to say, but not very many, and when a cooperative enterprise strives to get people who will serve the whole group, people who do not think that success can be measured in dollars but know that real success comes from serving a group and in having the supreme satisfaction of seeing the standard of living steadily raised, whether it be in a rural or urban community, it is very hard to find that kind of person. All these things make it very difficult to make a cooperative enterprise successful. I think one of the casualties of this depression was A. J. McPhail, president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. Speaking of cooperation he says:
The prospect of greater financial returns alone is not enough. Unselfishness, the spirit of sacrifice, the spirit of fair play, of "do unto others as you would that they should do unto you," of kindness-these qualities make a great and lasting appeal to the hearts and imaginations of men. Cooperation in its best and truest sense stands for all of these.
Again he says:
Cooperation is a combination of the practical and the ideal. It offers ample scope for putting into practice the ideas of the practical man as well as the ideals of the idealist. It is not only the most efficient, economical and practical way of doing business but when carried to its ultimate conclusion it recognizes equality and the interdependence of all human beings. It provides a business medium through which progressive and socially minded men and women wth high ideals can find satisfaction and peace of mind in useful work. It is revolutionary in that it aims to bring about a more equitable distribution of wealth by returning to its members as nearly as possible the full value of the product of their labour.

It may be news to you that while some of the prairie provinces have had difficulty in selling their bonds at a reasonable price. Manitoba recently completed the sale of $5,000,000 worth at five per cent.

budget, at the same time taking care to point out the large deficit faced by the federal government. The fifth allegation against this government is that the offer of a commission was not applicable because there was no three-year crop failure area in Manitoba. Let me point out that the commission set up in Saskatchewan, as noted in the correspondence we now have on Hansard, were looking after the "A" area, the "B" area and the "C" area- that is, those areas where there were respectively three crop failures, tw'o crop failures and one crop failure.
It is pointed out also that there was a lack of knowledge on the part of the province of Manitoba. That is the sixth allegation. May I point out that the province of Manitoba could merely have taken down the telephone and asked the government of Saskatchewan how they were handling the relief question, and could have had the answer. It is said that the province of Manitoba has received orphan treatment from this government. The only orphans in the picture are the farmers of the drought area of Manitoba. They are the orphans that have not been fairly treated by the province of Manitoba. I repeat, they are the only orphans in the picture. The responsibility, so far as the federal government is concerned, was pointed out, I think, very well by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), when he spoke in this house on April 3, 1930. It is agreed in this house that the responsibility is, first, on the municipality, and when it cannot function then it is upon the province; and finally, if the province cannot function, the federal government has the responsibility. That responsibility the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta have accepted, and they have carried on and given feed and fodder relief to the farmers. Manitoba, of course, was unprepared, in spite of the information which they had from the different municipalities of which I know. On January 15 they had no estimate in regard to feed for their cattle. Then they changed their estimate on January 30, February 19 and February 24, on three different occasions, showing that they had taken no trouble to consolidate the information which had been received from the different municipalities in order to place it properly before the federal government.
It, is pointed out that there is a limit to credit so far as the different governments are concerned. May I point out to the house that there is a limitation of credit for every individual, for every municipality, for every province and for every dominion, and unfortunately some dominions have gone beyond that limit. If in the province of Manitoba, as it is alleged, they are in excellent financial condition, then they are able to look after the farmers in the drought area perhaps even better than is the case in Saskatchewan or Alberta.
The chief difficulty, which may be seen throughout the entire picture, is this: At present the government in Manitoba is facing a provincial election which must be fought on federal issues. The premier of Manitoba criticizes this government in regard to unemployment, in regard to its agricultural policy, in regard to the deficit, in regard to old age pensions, in regard to the financing of relief and in regard to the lack of markets. I say to this house and to this country that it is unfair to the farmers of the district I represent that we have in the province of Manitoba a man who, while seeking aid from the federal government, at the same time criticizes that government in regard to its policies. I point to the premier of Alberta, who does no such thing. I say that is unfortunate and I know for the last six months I have been up against that difficulty, of having a man asking for help and at the same time criticizing those who are helping him.
I note that I have not a great deal of time left, but I want to point out that because of these conditions and because the farmers within that area have not been assisted by the provincial government, in my opinion conditions there at present are worse than they are in any other place in western Canada. In
The Budget-Mr. Willis

that connection I want to point out also, as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) pointed out, that this is a great and productive area. There is no lack of productivity of the soil; this condition exists for the same reason that a similar condition exists in Saskatchewan. Soil which for years gave crops is not doing so at present, and has not done so for the last two years because of drought. The farmers who are in that area are as efficient as the farmers in any part of Canada, but the drought is responsible for their condition.
In nothing that I say do I relieve this government of its real responsibility towards the people. It has a real responsibility to the farmers who live in my district, but so far -I know nothing of the future-I have sought in vain to find out in what way this government has not lived up to its responsibility in this regard. It is my considered opinion-and if it were not so I would not say it-that this government has fulfilled its constitutional responsibility and that necessarily the fault must lie with the government of Manitoba. The situation is unfortunate; within that area many cattle and horses have died. The horses remaining are in such condition that it will require more feed and much more care to bring them back to normal. They are so weak at present that they cannot do a full day's work, and they will not be able to do a full day's work when seeding comes along.
I think it is unfortunate that any question of politics should come up in regard to the responsibilities of the municipalities, the province and the dominion. The municipalities have worked hard to do what was possible for the people within their borders, but the municipalities have reached the end of their financial resources and now they must look to the province and the dominion for aid. I think the municipalities have fulfilled their responsibility to their own people.
The hon. gentleman has spoken for forty minutes.

They were somewhat along the line of some figures which I intended to quote, but I want to pay .my hon. friend the compliment of saying that conditions as she pictured them are worse under the present administration than I had intended to show. If I correctly recall the figure she gave, it showed a decrease of something over 50 per cent in the price of agricultural products. The information I was able to obtain shows that the decrease was just a little under 50 per cent, but I have not the slightest doubt that she is correct, so I give her the benefit of the doubt. Make it 25 per cent.

My hon. friend is now
thinking of interest rates.
While the price of what the farmers have to buy has decreased less than fifteen per cent, the price of what they have to sell has decreased by more than one-half.
I should like to refer as rapidly as I can to two or three matters, although they have already been mentioned in the brilliant address delivered by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston). First of all, let me point out that the budget shows that the trade of Canada this last year is just a little over $26,000,000, less than one-half of what it was two years ago when our hon. friends said that conditions were very bad. May I also call attention to the fact that the
funded debt in the last two years has increased by about $307,000,000. The decrease brought about in the funded debt by the government led by my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) during the last five years that government was in office, amounted to $257,000,000, and unfortunately we hear now from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) that they have eaten up in two years the amount by which the former government reduced the debt in five years, and about $50,000,000 besides. Apparently under some governments deficits are such a common occurrence and amount to such enormous proportions that it is pretty difficult to realize how great they are. May I draw attention to the fact that the increase in the funded debt of Canada during the past two years is within about $30,000,000 of the total debt before the war? Before the war the total debt amounted to $336,000,000, so that the increase that has taken place in the past couple of years would almost equal the total debt prior to the war.
I regret to say that the budget delivered by my hon. friend is, I believe, the most terrible one that has ever been given to the house, not excluding the budgets that were delivered during the war years, because it was realized then that a war was in progress. During that period the deficits some years were very large, but the large deficits came practically after the war was over, while we were in the reconstruction period. The deficit, however, in the present budget is the largest shown in any budget that has ever been delivered in the house with the exception of the war years or the years immediately succeeding the war. Those are some of the things to which I think the attention of the public should be directed at this time.
What perhaps is the best test of the condition of the country is the bank debits. The figures are as follows:

It can thus be seen what a tremendous decrease has taken place. To-day the farmer is selling his grain, cattle and dairy produce, about which the hon. member for Souris was so eloquent during the last election-, for from 21 to 30 per cent less than he did two years ago, but as the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth pointed out, when the farmer goes to buy boots and shoes for his children, he pays only 4-6 per cent less for them now than he did two years ago.
Another interesting point about the present budget is this-and I am not blaming the
The Budget-Mr. Elliott

present Minister of Finance for all of it, because he had charge of the department, not for the whole year but for only a very small part of it. The sales tax, which is a most important one, last year realized much less than one-half of the estimate. That is not good financing and is not creditable to the manner in which the country has lived up to the expectation of the right hon. gentleman who introduced the budget a year ago.
Perhaps of all the bad features of the present budget, the worst is what is called an increase of two per cent in the excise tax. That is a tariff; there is no question about that. I do not know what is the idea of trying to disguise it by calling it an excise tax, which it is not. It is a tax which will bear heavily on all the people of this country, and bear heavily upon them in a way which cannot be estimated. It is one of the heaviest burdens than can be imposed. When a country gets into the condition in which this government finds this country at the present time after it has been in office for a year and eight months, it should be heroic enough to take steps that will compel those who have the ability to pay, to pay sufficient to get the country out of its financial difficulties. Wealth does not come to the people of any country entirely through their own unaided efforts. The man who has made a great fortune in Canada or any other country has made it partly of course by his own endeavours, but very largely by reason of the opportunities that have been afforded to him by the country in which he lives. At a time of crisis like this, is it too much to ask of the men with whom this country has dealt so kindly that they shall contribute not a small portion such as the government proposes in this budget, but a very substantial proportion of their wealth to help the country out of its present condition and if possible get it back on the road to prosperity. These men will again have the same opportunities they had in the past to make money, which they cannot do as conditions now are.,
I would ask the Minister of Finance why it is that in the budget, with the admission as to how bad conditions are in this country, there is no suggestion of any remedy. The only suggested remedy is to make the masses of the people pay more taxes. Mr. Speaker, the common people are not in a position to pay more taxes. I happen to know them pretty well, particularly those in the section in which I live, and during the last six months more of the best farmers that live in this dominion have come to me and told me that they did not know how in the world 
they were going to get the money to pay their taxes, than in all the rest of the time I have known them. Many who five or six years ago were among the best, most prosperous and enterprising farmers in that community are to-day on the verge of bankruptcy, because the man who was enterprising and courageous four or five years ago perhaps bought another farm for his boy or built a barn or got himself into debt. There is one thing which has not come down in price in this country, Mr. Speaker, and that is the rate of interest which people have to pay on the money they borrowed some years ago or have to borrow to-day. I know something about the way interest works, and I know that it accumulates to-day just as it did when times were prosperous. A great many of the people in this country who borrowed money four or five years ago are to-day unable to pay even the interest. I am fairly intimate with a certain party who has sold several farms and know how conditions are with him; in fact many of our farmers to-day are not only unable to pay off any principal, but are also unable to meet the interest, and many of them are not able to pay even taxes on their farms.
This government came into office less than two years ago-it seems a lot longer than that to the people of this country, but it was only a year and eight months ago-on the greatest group of promises ever made by any party in an election campaign in any country since elections were first- started, promises which I think were never exceeded for their absolute lack of limit. The Conservative party in its election campaign proposed certain definite remedies which were going to cure conditions not within a year or two, but almost immediately-in a few days, a few weeks or a few months. It was explained very clearly from every platform from which the Prime Minister and those who were with him spoke in that election that in a country situated as Canada was, different from almost any other country in the world, there was no reason why the people should not be prosperous if the government was doing its duty. This government has been in office nearly two years now, and it seems that the longer they are in power, the worse conditions get. What would the people of Canada not give to go back to the conditions that obtained only two years ago, when our friends opposite were going around the country telling the farmers and the manufacturers and the people in every walk of life how badly off they were.
Why have conditions become so much worse since the present government -came into power?

The Budget-Mr. Elliott
There is no question that world conditions have exercised a certain influence, just as they were exercising a certain influence upon the affairs of Canada during the last election when our friends would not admit that world conditions had anything to do with our economic affairs.
I want to call attention to what I think may assist the government, if they will be assisted, in getting this country out of the position in which we are now placed. We have been building up in this country for a great many years now a fiscal policy. That policy has been built up by great men, the leaders of finance and commerce in this country, and in order that my hon. friends opposite may know just how far they have departed from the policies which they claim to be following, may I call attention to a resolution which was introduced into this house on the eighteenth of January, 1911, by Hon. Arthur Meighen, now the government leader in the upper house? His resolution reads:
That in the opinion of this house, a substantial reduction in the import duties on agricultural implements is now due the agriculturists of Canada, and is in just accord with the true ends of a protective tariff.
That was in 1911. He followed that up by saying:
I hope to bring home to the government this afternoon that in their attempts to continue the National Policy which had obtained for years before, they have overlooked, they have neglected one essential feature of that policy, they have quite forgotten its guiding principle, namely, the principle that as our industrial institutions advanced in strength and as they were able with every advance to acquire a hold on the home market, the import duties were to be diminished and adjusted in order to meet the evolving and changing conditions.
Then Mr. Meighen quoted the words of the father of the national policy, Sir John A. Macdonald, who in 1878 used the following words:
If we had a protective system in this country, if we had a developed capital, we could, by giving our manufacturers a reasonable hold on our home trade, attain a higher position among the nations. I do not mean that we should adopt a tariff like that of the United States, but one such as the necessities of Canada demand.
Then he quotes further from the words of Sir John A. Macdonald:
It can well be understood that a judicious tariff may, on the whole, be a moderate tariff.
Then the present leader of the upper house went on to say:
So that the basic principle was laid down in so far as the feature I am now emphasizing goes, was that the object of that tariff was to give the manufacturing industries of Canada a
reasonable hold on the home market. The same principle was supported by Sir Leonard Tilley at page 429 of Hansard, 1879.
And he also mentions that it was supported by Mr. Foster who in the year 1894 used these words:
If there is to be a protective system at all, everybody knows that it must be higher in its inception than as the years gradually pass, when industries have become established and when the industrial development of the country grows apace.
And then Mr. Meighen goes on to quote the words of the Hon. John Haggart and others.
I am about to quote from the speech from the throne which was presented on February 15, 1921, at a time when the present leader of the Senate was Prime Minister. The following words were used:
It is the opinion of my advisers that in such revision regard must be had to the necessities of revenue and as well that the principle of protection to Canadian labour and legitimate Canadian industries, including agriculture, which has prevailed for more than forty years in this country, must be consistently maintained: but that the customs duties imposed to that end should be no higher than is essential to ensure good standards of living among our working population and to retain and make possible the normal expansion of the industries in which they find employment.
One would have thought, looking over the increase in the public debt of this country and seeing that in 1920 it had increased by about $674,000,000, that if financial conditions were going to be cured by increased tariffs this country needed such advantages at that time as badly as it does now. The point I wish to make is that in the changes in tariff which took place in 1930 and again last year the leader of this government, and the hon. members who followed him, departed entirely from the principles of the national policy as enunciated by Conservative leaders of the past. The national policy was one of protection for industries until they got on a sound footing and were able to compete with outside industries of a similar nature. The provisions of the present Canadian tariff practically prohibit from entering Canada goods which can be produced in Canada. The condition is so serious that I think the house should have from the government some statement as to how long they propose continuing with the experiment of prohibitive tariffs, and how long they are going to allow this country to go back financially by leaps and bounds as they have been doing since they came into power. The country cannot stand such a policy for many years. The high tariff legislation has been in force for a year and eight months,
The Budget-Mr. Elliott

and judging from the speech of the Minister of Finance I would say that there is not much hope of a change, because in this budget he is levying duties which were not thought of a year ago. That is a position which is very serious, so far as Canadians are concerned. It will be quite impossible for some industries to carry on unless a change is made.
One hears a good deal about the Imperial economic conference; I hope that it will produce some good results. It was interesting to note that the Minister of Finance said he did not think it advisable to make any substantial changes in the tariff in view of the impending conference. I should like to ask him this question: What is the difference in that respect between this conference and the last one? We know that just before the last conference nearly all the items in the Canadian tariff schedules were jacked up. I am glad to see the Prime Minister in his seat, because I think he more than anybody else is responsible for the increases in tariff which have taken place. I believe he had some voice in the proceedings which took place when the present budget was being formulated. Why is it necessary to put into the budget speech the statement that in view of the pending conference it is not thought advisable to make any substantial tariff changes?
I wish to say only a few words more with regard to tariff changes which have taken place, and in that connection I should like to read from the Eastern Chronicle of October 20, 1931. That newspaper quotes the Ottawa Journal, which I am sure should appeal to my right hori. friend the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance. It is as follows:
From the statements of Hon. Mr. Cahan it is clear therefore that what the Dominion government has done is to place tariff on large classes of British goods of from 40 to 50 per cent, according to fluctuations in the value of the pound sterling.
The editorial is quite lengthy, and time will not permit me to read it all I should like to submit the following for the particular benefit of the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister:
That any manufacturer established under our tariff should as part of his business prepare himself to face changes in world trade and finance without rushing to Ottawa for more tariff when new circumstances do not suit him.
That a tariff on importation of 40 to 50 per cent is too high a tariff under almost any circumstances, and is particularly objectionable upon British go.ods.
Under present world conditions and particularly under the specific conditions which Canada has to face commercially and industrially, it seems to the [DOT]Tournal that the prin-

ciple and practice of tariff protection is necessary for this country. But it should be reasonable protection. There may he wisdom in giving a good tariff advantage to our manufacturers and other producers. But there cannot be wisdom in setting up a tariff advantage for anybody so great that it can be relied on to furnish a profit at the expense of our own people for manufacturing or production for which this country has no natural advantage, or for business which does not enjoy good management. ... a man's pocket lias a fierce influence on his logic. As for the Journal, our creed is that an industry in Canada which cannot get along with a moderate tariff advantage should not be in this country at all.
I submit one of the great reasons for the condition in this country to-day is the tariff system which has been introduced, a system contrary to the policies of my right hon. friend's predecessors, contrary to the policy followed since the 'national policy was first introduced.
With regard to the imperial conference I have this particularly to say to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister and to the Minister of Finance. I read from the former's speech on the budget of 1930, page 1825 of Hansard:
If a dollar goes to the West Indies that should go to a Canadian, it is no better than if the money went to the United States.
That statement was made in the campaign when the British preference introduced by Mr. Dunning was an issue.
I was interested also in reading some .remarks by Sir Josiah Stamp. He needs no introduction to the people of this country and particularly to the Prime Minister. It was a distinct privilege for many members of this house and the Senate to hear him in an address he delivered in this building a short time ago. I quote this extract from that address as reported in the Montreal Gazette of April 8, 1932:
"Two thoughts I would leave with you about the Imperial conference," said Josiah Stamp in his concluding remarks. "As an economist I would ask politicians to listen to me. If you have a solution of a thing, or a scheme, or the result of a bargain which is a fine thing for yourself but not so good for the other man, if that is tiie way it works out, my experience is that no such bargain ever pans out that way. It cannot be lasting. Such bargains have a terrible nemesis within them.
"I dread to think that the wonderful sentiment of empire should ever be tested by material results. Never by arithmetic should we say a thing is good or bad for the empire. Never must the empire rest upon a mere economic connection that is purely mercenary or materialistic. We require, in arranging for empire trade and relations, not only a wise judgment but a long judgment. Do not let us go into this Imperial conference with any shortsighted penny-wise-and-pound-foolish idea. I believe the British empire is and can be the greatest economic and moral force in the world to-day. We are engaged in rebuilding the

The Budget-Mr. Mullins
world, in rebuilding society, after a military and financial disintegration. In that great task the British empire must lead the way, to the end that 'out of its ashes strong as the morning springeth the new'."
I should like to place alongside those words the passage with which Mr. Dunning concluded his budget speech in 1930 so that hon. members may see how closely the two statements correspond. That, I submit, is the sentiment that should govern in approaching the economic conference. I cannot think that it was good business at a time like this to impose what is called an excise tax, which is really a tax against all goods coming from Great Britain. That was not the kind of friendly gesture that I think makes for success in such a conference. I do hope, Mr. Speaker, that the economic conference will be productive of much good, I do hope, if it does nothing else, that the multitude of wise men who will then be gathered together will be able to point out to the members of this government the economic folly of a tariff that means prohibition of imports and not merely protection for the industries of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I have been sitting in this house for some time listening to hon. gentlemen opposite, and I have yet to find one constructive suggestion coming from them; every word has been a.word of criticism. I have been listening to the old story of the tariff. How they have been bolstering it up for political purposes so they may have political propaganda when they go to the country later on! I have lived under every Prime Minister from Sir John A. Macdonald down to the present right hon. gentleman who occupies the position, and I never knew one of them who ever took office under the same conditions as confronted the present Prime Minister. You left on our doorstep a lot of problems that were very hard to handle. We on this side of the house have done everything possible to help out the situation. I remember quite well how the right hon. leader of the opposition went up and down the country asking for more support, to be given a larger representation in this house in order that he might have an adequate majority independent of the Progressives. But a majority was given to this side of the house. We have a working majority and when measures come up we can put them through.
I have heard a great deal of the old story called the tariff from the apostles of free trade. But I wonder where they come in. The tariff under hon. gentlemen opposite was reduced. I admit it. But they raised the valuation for duty purposes. Let me illustrate. On a hundred dollar binder you reduced the tariff to six per cent, but you raised the valuation for duty purposes to $114. That misled the people all through the western country; they were not actually paying only a six per cent duty on their binder, as they were led to believe. Every prime minister has had to have a tariff. And the tariff is a good thing fox this country; it has prospered under a tariff. What did Abraham Lincoln say? Listen to this:
I do not know much about tariff, but I do know this much-when we buy goods from a foreign country, we get the goods and the foreigner gets the money; but when we buy goods made at home, we get both the goods and the money.
Can you prove that Lincoln ever said that?
No, it is attributed to Robert Ingersoll.

It is written in history as I have given it. But I can prove what this gentleman said because I heard him; I refer to President Hoover:
The most urgent economic problem in our day is agriculture. An adequate tariff is the foundation of farm relief. The domestic market must be protected. I would use my office to give farmers the full benefit of our historic tariff policy.
That speech was made at Palo Alto in California on August 11, 1928.
An hen. MEMBER: He has changed his mind since.

I happened to be down there at the time, I was not then a member of this house. Then what about the right hon. leader of the opposition? Speaking at Kingston, Ontario, he said:
We realize that our industries here have to have safeguards with respect to competition from other parts of the world, competition from the country to the south of us, competition from conditions as they are in England, and we think that is all the more reason why these days of depreciated currency and the like we should have the benefit of expert advice and information on all these great questions on the tariff.
That was the statement made by the leader of the opposition when touring this country. I have another statement, one made by the Hon. Charles Dunning. Mr. Dunning said, "I am no free trader". I heard him at the town of Yorkton say he was advocating free trade. He was a free trader there, but in the following article he says that he is no free trader. Let me quote:
"I am no free trader. If Saskatchewan were all of Canada then free trade might be good, but it is not all of Canada, neither is Ontario.
The Budget-Mr. Mullins

It is because of the difficulty of getting a national tariff policy and making it a practical, not a political matter."-These observations of Mr. Dunning embrace a whole flock of surprises.
It is surprising to learn for the first time and from his own lips that he is no free trader. It is equally surprising to have his admission that Saskatchewan is not all of Canada. It is positively startling to be informed from such a source that the tariff should not be regarded as a political matter. Mr. Dunning is assuredly stepping out. Can it be that he has fallen in with bad company in the wicked east?
That appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune.
Now, before I resume my seat I am going to ask for more protection, and this will seem a rather strange flower to come from the prairies. But I am going to put myself on record as asking, in aid of agriculture, more protection than we have. I want one of the principal products of the farm to have some protection. I want the live stock industry to be protected. For instance, we are bringing in 50,000 cattle and shipping out about 25,000 or 30,000. You will ask me in what way I want protection for the live stock of this country. I have heard it said by hon. members on the other side that prices are going down gradually. I admit it; they have gone down. But I say to them, you have gone down in quality; you have no export cattle at all. What is driving down prices is this. We are bringing in 10,000,000 pounds of canned meats from the Argentine, and how are we bringing in those canned meats? In this way. We are bringing in the front quarters. When they slaughter their cattle in the Argentine they take the hind quarters and cut them what they call long-I am talking on a subject I know something about, because I had money invested in that country in a packing concern -and they ship the hind quarters to England and then can the front quarters, and that meat comes in to Canada in great quantities in competition with our live stock, thus driving prices down. I may be asked how I arrive at the estimate I have given of 50,000 cattle. Perhaps some hon. members may know something about this business; I believe the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan) has some knowledge along this line. Well, take a 1,000 pound steer and dress it, and you will find that the average steer will dress 500 pounds of beef. Take the bones from that meat so as to get the meat ready for canning and you have 200 pounds of beef ready to put into cans. If, therefore, you bring into the country
10,000,000 pounds of canned meats you are bringing in the equivalent of 50,000 cattle. Now, I want the government, by order in council, under the authority we have given them in this house, to adopt some sort of pro-

tective tariff to stop that meat coming into Canada. I also want them to do the same thing in regard to the bringing in of pickled pork. A large quantity of that product is brought in and some of it comes in free. A good deal has been said about the price of hogs being lowered. Yes; the price of hogs is being lowered by the importation of vegetable oil that is brought in from the south, providing work for coloured labour in the southern country, and it is brought here and manufactured into a shortening called Crisco. We import something like 89,760,400 pounds of this article which takes the place of lard. Lard is a five per cent better shortening than this product, which is a deodorized oil, the odor being taken out by the Wesson process. It is not as healthy a food as lard derived from well fed Canadian hogs-and we have the best hogs in Canada, fed under our conditions. Any man who has ever been in Illinois or Iowa will know how they feed their hogs there, but the hogs in Canada produce a better iard than this imported shortening. I would ask the government to impose a good, stiff, heavy duty in order to shut that product out of this country. I submit that this should be done in the interests of farming in Canada. I find also that there is a good deal of barrel pork coming into this country. Why should wTe import barrel pork in competition with our farmers who are producing hogs? The Atlantic and Pacific stores in Toronto brought in two carloads of hams from Chicago and knocked the price of bacon down very low. The result was that the hog market in Toronto was affected that day when these hams were imported.

Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
